# The Night Is a Country

At 4:31 on the morning of January 17, 1994, an earthquake struck Los Angeles. Named for the suburb at its epicenter, the Northridge quake broke freeways, dropped apartment buildings onto their own parking lots, and cut electrical power across huge swaths of the city. What followed was, among other things, an unplanned experiment. For the first time in living memory, Los Angeles went truly dark — not dim, not browned out, but dark down to the streets and up to the sky. People stumbled out of their houses, because that is what you do after an earthquake: you get to open ground and look around. And a number of them looked up and saw something vast and pale arched over the city, a grainy river of light unlike anything they had ever seen. In the days that followed, emergency operators and observatory staff fielded calls about it. People wanted to know what the giant silvery cloud was, and whether it was dangerous.

It was the Milky Way. Their own galaxy. A hundred billion suns arranged in a disk so wide that light itself needs a hundred thousand years to cross it, seen edge-on from the inside, from a quiet arm where a small yellow star keeps a small blue planet. The callers had lived their entire lives inside that structure and beneath its glow, and they did not recognize it when they were finally shown it.

For roughly every human generation before theirs — for every person who ever lived until, say, the middle of the twentieth century — that river was as familiar as the moon. Herders watched it. Sailors steered by it. It runs through the myths of every continent and the oldest songs we have. A 2016 atlas of artificial sky brightness found that the Milky Way is now hidden from more than a third of humanity, including sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans. And here is the detail I can't shake: darkness did not take the sky away from us. Light did. Light spilling up from parking lots and billboards, scattering off the air and hanging there like bright dust, until the sky above a city glows faintly orange at midnight and shows only a handful of the boldest stars. We didn't lose the night. We filled it in, the way you fill in a wetland, and called the result progress.

Night used to be a country people actually lived in, with its own customs, and one of those customs has been almost forgotten. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years reading court transcripts, diaries, letters, sermons, and medical texts from the centuries before electric light, and he kept running into a strange phrase: *first sleep*. It turns up in Chaucer, in Cervantes, in divorce depositions, in shepherd's almanacs. The pattern it points to was so ordinary that no one thought to explain it. People went to bed not long after dark and slept a few hours. Then, somewhere around midnight, they woke — not from worry, but naturally, the way a person wakes in the morning — and entered an interval of quiet wakefulness that sources call the watch. In the watch, people prayed. They got up to relieve themselves. They tended the fire, split kindling, smoked a pipe, talked softly, made love. Some rose and visited neighbors by moonlight. Some simply lay still and thought, or discussed the dreams of the first sleep, which were considered worth discussing. After an hour or two, they went back down into a second sleep and rose at dawn.

For a long time this was assumed to be a cultural artifact, a habit of firelit centuries. Then, in the early nineties, the sleep researcher Thomas Wehr ran a kind of reverse experiment: he gave a group of adult volunteers fourteen hours of darkness every night for a month — roughly what a winter night once offered — and watched what happened. By the fourth week, without being instructed to, the volunteers had reorganized their sleep into two distinct shifts, separated by a serene interval of wakefulness in the middle of the night. Samples taken during that interval showed elevated prolactin, a marker of calm. The subjects described the state as something like drowsy contemplation — not insomnia, not anxiety, just a quiet the modern schedule never gives anyone. The watch, it turns out, may still be in us, folded up like a vestigial organ, waiting for enough darkness to unfold.

This is the reframe I keep returning to. Most of us have met the watch without knowing its name: you surface at three in the morning, oddly awake, and lie there with a mind that will not re-engage and will not shut off. We call this insomnia, a disorder — and sometimes it is. But the historical record suggests that a wakeful hour in the middle of the night is closer to an inheritance than an error, an appointment our species kept for millennia. The modern mistake isn't waking at 3 a.m. It's what we do next: reach for the phone, flood the eyes with blue light, check the world's pulse and take it personally, then lie there in a chemical daylight of our own making, wondering why sleep won't come back. Our ancestors had a protocol for this hour. It involved no screens, and it considered thinking in the dark to be one of the uses of a night.

The machinery by which we unmade the night arrived in stages, each one reasonable. For most of history, artificial light meant fire — a rushlight, a splinter of pine, a tallow candle that smelled of rendering and cost roughly an hour's wage to burn. A candle was money on fire; the poor simply went to bed. Then came lamps burning whale oil, which is the part of the story people forget: the great whaling fleets of the early nineteenth century were, at bottom, a lighting industry, chasing the brightest fuel afloat. Then gas, which lit Pall Mall in 1807 and within decades had filled London with tens of thousands of street lamps lit on schedule — there was an official hour called "lighting-up time," and a profession of men with poles who went ahead of dusk, setting the city on fire in small, careful doses. Then Edison, and the incandescent bulb, which made light so cheap that the constraint stopped being fuel and became only fixture. The word *curfew* comes from *couvre-feu* — "cover the fire" — the bell that once ordered a town to bank its flames and sleep. Our version rings at last call.

Each stage shortened the night. What had been a country with its own customs became a poorly lit annex of the day, then a fully serviced one: night shifts, night flights, diners, freeways, a world advertised as 24/7 as though the number itself were an achievement. Along the way we changed what darkness means. It used to be a season of the day, dangerous and fertile. Now it reads as underproduction — downtime, vacancy, undeveloped acreage, unrealized gross domestic product. A dark parking lot looks like money lying on the ground. That is why the lights stay on all night above empty offices: not because anyone is there, but because brightness has become a synonym for use, and use a synonym for virtue.

That same atlas found that more than eighty percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies. Consider what the sky was before that: the one commons that could not be enclosed, the one possession distributed perfectly equally, owned by no one and within reach of everyone — the beggar and the emperor saw the same stars, and the stars neither knew nor cared which was which. We managed, in about a century, to raise a fence of glare around even that. The good news is stranger than the bad: light pollution is the only environmental catastrophe with an off switch. Smog takes decades to clear; an extinct species stays extinct. But the night sky is still up there, fully intact, undamaged, waiting the way it has waited all along. Flip the switches, and it returns the same evening.

Your eyes know this even if you don't. Vision at night runs on different equipment than vision by day: cones for color and detail, rods for dimness, and the rods pay for their sensitivity with slowness. Their light-catching chemistry, a pigment called rhodopsin, is so delicate that a single flash of white light wipes it out, and so slow to rebuild that full dark adaptation takes about half an hour. This is why astronomers carry red flashlights — the rods are nearly blind to deep red, so you can read a star chart without spending your darkness. It is also why the phone you check at 2 a.m. is such a strange instrument: in three seconds of screen, you liquidate a treasury that took thirty minutes to accumulate, and then you wonder why the room feels smaller. Darkness, in other words, is not a simple absence. It is a capacity. It is something the eye maintains, like a muscle or a balance, and we go around casually spending it.

We are also, it bears repeating, the unusual ones. Humans are diurnal primates, a daytime exception on a planet that is mostly nocturnal: by most counts, the majority of mammal species do their living in the dark, along with uncountable insects — the entire night shift of the living world. When we light the night for our convenience, we are not illuminating an empty room. Sea turtle hatchlings, hardwired to scramble toward the brighter horizon — which for a hundred million years meant moonlight on the sea — now crawl inland toward beachfront glow and die on highways. Migrating birds navigate by stars and skylines both, and estimates of the number killed in collisions with lit buildings in the United States alone run into the hundreds of millions each year. Even the moth at your porch light, the oldest joke in the natural world, turns out not to be a fool in love with a flame: high-speed cameras show that artificial light trips the ancient reflex that keeps an insect's back to the sky, so the moth banks around your bulb as if it were the horizon of a tiny, catastrophic world. We have strobe-lit the other half of the biosphere and called it safety.

But the loss I feel most keenly is not up there; it is in here. Anyone who has lain awake at 3 a.m. knows that night has a chemistry of thought all its own. The daytime mind is a defended mind — scheduled, armored, moving forward on rails of intention. In the dark, the rails lift. Memories surface without being asked. A grief you filed under *things to feel later* arrives and insists on being felt now; a plan you were proud of looks thin; an old love walks through the room without knocking, and you let it, because in the dark there is nothing to prove. Our ancestors had a standing appointment with this mind, every midnight, and treated it as a normal organ of life — the watch was where you took stock, prayed, let the dreams of the first sleep settle into words. We medicalized the appointment, then abolished the place where it was kept.

None of which is to say the old dark was gentle. It was dangerous in ways we have forgotten down to our nerves: predators and intruders, fire in a thatched village, illness at 2 a.m., and the simple unknown of whatever was out past the firelight. Folklore is the sediment of that danger — revenants, the Wild Hunt, the hour when the dead were permitted to visit. Here is the paradox we live in now: we abolished the dangers and kept the fear, and lost the familiarity that made fear bearable. Night used to be feared and known, a country with customs. It is now neither feared with reason nor known at all — just brightly, continuously lit, the way you would light a room you were afraid to enter.

And yet the old night had one thing our lit one lacks. Sleep is the great democracy; unconsciousness does not check credentials. The emperor and the shepherd lay down under the same gravity, dreamed by the same rules, woke into the same watch. Night was the one time the hierarchy of the visible world dissolved — maybe one reason the powerful historically distrusted it, since assemblies, conspiracies, and revivals all meet after dark. There is a kind of leveling that happens only when the lights go out, and we have been quietly voting against it for two centuries.

There is a final irony in the sky itself. It looks eternal, but it is not even still. The pole star, Polaris, holds a temporary appointment: in about twelve thousand years the earth's wobbling axis will point near Vega, and a different star will stand over the north. The constellations are drifting drawings; give the Big Dipper a hundred thousand years and it will be unrecognizable. You cannot miss a country you were never told exists.

# The Night Is a Country

At 4:31 on the morning of January 17, 1994, an earthquake struck Los Angeles. Named for the suburb at its epicenter, the Northridge quake broke freeways, dropped apartment buildings onto their own parking lots, and cut electrical power to huge swaths of the city. What followed was, among other things, an unplanned experiment. For the first time in living memory, Los Angeles went truly dark — not dim, not browned out, but dark down to the streets and up to the sky. People stumbled out of their houses, because that is what you do after an earthquake: you get to open ground and look around. And a number of them looked up and saw something vast and pale arched over the city, a grainy river of light unlike anything they had ever seen. In the days that followed, emergency operators and observatory staff fielded calls about it. People wanted to know what the giant silvery cloud was, and whether it was dangerous.

It was the Milky Way. Their own galaxy. A hundred billion suns arranged in a disk so wide that light itself needs a hundred thousand years to cross it, seen edge-on from the inside, from a quiet arm where a small yellow star keeps a small blue planet. The callers had lived their entire lives inside that structure and under its glow, and they did not recognize it when they were finally shown it.

But the loss I feel most keenly is not up there; it is in here. Anyone who has lain awake at 3 a.m. knows that night has a chemistry of thought all its own. It is now neither feared with reason nor known at all — just brightly, continuously lit, the way you'd light a room you were afraid to enter.

And yet the old night had one thing our lit one lacks. Sleep is the great democracy; unconsciousness does not check credentials. The emperor and the shepherd lay down under the same gravity, dreamed by the same rules, woke into the same watch. Night was the one time the hierarchy of the visible world dissolved, which is maybe one reason the powerful historically distrusted it — assemblies, conspiracies, and revivals all meet after dark. There is a kind of leveling that only happens when the lights go out, and we have been quietly voting against it for two centuries.

There's a final irony in the sky itself. It looks eternal, but it is not even still. The pole star, Polaris, is a temporary appointment: in about twelve thousand years the earth's axis will have wobbled around to point near Vega, and a different star will stand over the north. We speak of darkness as absence, and the word itself cooperates — un-lit, de-prived. But the deepest seeing we do requires it. On a truly dark night, from a dark coast, you can see the Andromeda galaxy with your naked eye: a trillion stars, two and a half million light-years away, the farthest thing visible without a lens. The faintest light in the universe is visible only to a fully dark-adapted eye under a fully dark sky, which is to say: the reach of human sight is bought with darkness, spent from darkness, paid for in the very thing we are erasing. That is why the lights stay on all night above empty offices, why billboards need to be visible from orbit: not because anyone is there, but because brightness has become a synonym for use, and use a synonym for virtue.

(~120)

P9 — commons:

The 2016 atlas I mentioned found that more than eighty percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies. Think about what the sky was before that: the one commons that could not be enclosed, the one possession distributed perfectly equally, owned by no one and in reach of everyone — the beggar and the emperor saw the same stars, and the stars neither knew nor cared which was which. We managed, in about a century, to put up a fence of glare around even that. The good news is stranger than the bad: light pollution is the only environmental catastrophe with an off switch. Smog takes decades to clear; a species, once extinct, stays extinct. But the night sky is still up there, fully intact, undamaged, waiting the way it has waited for all of it. Flip the switches, and it returns the same evening.

(~135)

P10 — physiology:

And your eyes know this, even if you don't. Vision at night runs on different equipment than vision by day: cones for color and detail, rods for dimness, and the rods pay for their sensitivity with slowness. Their light-catching chemistry, a pigment called rhodopsin, is so delicate that a single flash of white light wipes it out, and so slow to rebuild that full dark adaptation takes about half an hour. This is why astronomers carry red flashlights — the rods are nearly blind to deep red, so you can read a star chart without spending your darkness. It's also why the phone you check at 2 a.m. is such a strange instrument: in three seconds of screen, you liquidate a treasury that took thirty minutes to accumulate, and then you wonder why the room feels smaller. Darkness, in other words, is not a simple absence. It's a capacity. It's something the eye maintains, like a muscle or a balance, and we go around casually spending it.

(~165)

P11 — ecology:

We are also, it bears repeating, the unusual ones. Humans are diurnal primates, a daytime exception on a planet that is mostly nocturnal: by most counts, the majority of mammal species do their living in the dark, along with uncountable insects, moths, beetles, the entire night shift of the living world. When we light the night for our convenience, we are not illuminating an empty room. Sea turtle hatchlings, hardwired to scramble toward the brighter horizon — which, for a hundred million years, meant moonlight on the sea — now crawl inland toward beachfront glow and die on highways. Migrating birds navigate by stars and skylines both, and estimates of the number killed in collisions with lit buildings in the United States alone run into the hundreds of millions each year. Even the moth at your porch light, the oldest joke in the natural world, turns out not to be a fool in love with a flame: high-speed cameras show that the light trips the ancient reflex that keeps an insect's back to the sky, so the moth banks around your bulb as if it were the horizon of a tiny, catastrophic world. We have strobe-lit the other half of the biosphere and called it safety.

(~195)

P12 — interior night:

But the loss I feel most keenly is not up there; it is in here. Anyone who has lain awake at 3 a.m. knows that night has a chemistry of thought all its own. The daytime mind is a defended mind — scheduled, Armored, moving forward on rails of intention. In the dark, the rails lift. Memories surface without being asked. A grief you'd filed under things to feel later arrives and insists on being felt now; a plan you were proud of looks thin; an old love walks through the room without knocking, and you let it, because in the dark there is nothing to prove. Our ancestors had a standing appointment with this mind, every midnight, and treated it as a normal organ of life — the watch was where you took stock, prayed, let the dreams of the first sleep settle into words. We medicalized the appointment, then abolished the place where it was kept.

(~150)

P13 — fear/folklore:

None of which is to say the old dark was gentle. It was dangerous in ways we have forgotten down to our nerves: predators and intruders, fire in a thatched village, illness at 2 a.m., and the simple screaming unknown of what was out past the firelight. Folklore is the sediment of that danger — revenants, the Wild Hunt, the hour when the dead were allowed to visit. Here is the paradox we live in now: we abolished the dangers and kept the fear, and lost the familiarity that made fear bearable. Night used to be feared and known, a country with customs. It is now neither feared with reason nor known at all — just brightly, continuously lit, the way you'd light a room you were afraid to enter.

(~125)

P14 — democracy of sleep:

And yet the old night had one thing our lit one lacks. Sleep is the great democracy; unconsciousness does not check credentials. The emperor and the shepherd lay down under the same gravity, dreamed by the same rules, woke into the same watch. Night was the one time the hierarchy of the visible world dissolved, which is maybe one reason the powerful historically distrusted it — assemblies, conspiracies, and revivals all meet after dark. There is a kind of leveling that only happens when the lights go out, and we have been quietly voting against it for two centuries.

(~95)

P15 — drifting sky:

There's a final irony in the sky itself. It looks eternal, but it is not even still. The pole star, Polaris, is a temporary appointment: in about twelve thousand years the earth's axis will have wobbled around to point near Vega, and a different star will stand over the north. The constellations are drifting drawings; give the Big Dipper a hundred thousand years and it will be unrecognizable. So even "the same stars our ancestors saw" is only almost true — our descendants will inherit a subtly redrawn sky, and our ancestors inherited one slightly different from ours. But for the whole span of written memory, the sky was the one text every human generation could read, the oldest shared possession of a species scattered across every latitude and every century. When a child now grows up in a city glow and never once sees the Milky Way, the poverty is real, and it has the particular cruelty of the invisible: the child doesn't know anything was taken. You can't miss a country you were never told exists.

(~175)

P16 — darkness as presence:

We speak of darkness as absence, and the word itself cooperates — un-lit, de-prived. But the deepest seeing we do requires it. On a truly dark night, from a dark coast, you can see the Andromeda galaxy with your naked eye: a trillion stars, two and a half million light-years away, the farthest thing visible without a lens. You cannot see it by looking straight at it — the day-vision cones crowd the center of the retina — you must look slightly aside, letting the dim image fall on the rod-rich periphery, and hold still, and wait. The faintest light in the universe is visible only to a fully dark-adapted eye under a fully dark sky, which is to say: the reach of human sight is bought with darkness, spent from darkness, paid for in the very thing we are erasing. The night is not the world's off switch. It is the world's other half, where different things are true, and at this moment, as at every moment, half the planet is inside it. We just act like it isn't.

(~175)

P17 — modesty/practice:

A fair reader will object that this has been a romance. So it is, but let me be exact about what I'm defending. The lighting of the world bought real things: books read past dusk, streets made safer, surgeries performed at midnight, the whale, eventually, spared the lamp. The old dark was genuinely perilous, and I have no wish to send anyone back to it. The argument is narrower: there is a difference between lighting the night and erasing it, between light used and light spilled, and almost no one is choosing anymore — the spill is just the default setting of a civilization. Against that default, the resistance available to a person is almost embarrassingly small, and it works. Go outside on the next moonless night you can find. Turn nothing on. Stand there and do nothing for half an hour — the exact duration your rods require — and watch the sky deepen from black into its actual texture, which is grainy, layered, riverine, and vast. You will not be doing nothing. You will be repossessing, for free, land that was never lawfully taken.

(~180)

P18 — return to 1994:

This is why I keep thinking about those phone calls in Los Angeles. What moves me in the story is not that something new appeared in the sky that January night. Nothing new appeared. Every star over the freeway had been there the night before, and the night before that, over traffic reports and price wars and the whole bright noise of the city, patient beyond any human patience, doing the one thing it has always done, which is wait. The darkness was not the disaster. The darkness was the door, and for a few hours, all across a city built out of light, it stood open — and people walked through it, looked up at the enormous pale river of their own home, and had to call someone, anyone, just to ask: what is that? It's an excellent question. It is, in fact, the oldest one, and the night is where it lives.

(~150)
